title: Max Bottega: Keeping Art Direction interesting in a procedurally generated world
speaker: Max Bottega
talk_title: Keeping Art Direction interesting in a procedurally generated world
description: Italian-born Max is a Graphics Swiss Army Knife, with over 20 years in Art Direction and Animation production in video games. He’s worked across 20+ titles including Assetto Corsa, and most recently Cyberpunk 2077 as Lead Artist. In 2019 he decided to formally study Game Design at Vancouver Film School. Now returned to Europe, he lives in Hungary as co-Founder of Mac n Cheese Games, his second studio. He’s also an avid miniature painter, which shows in the care he takes for his game art.

segments.text: MAX: Hello. My name is Max Bottega. Today we will have a small talk on how to keep up the
interaction in the procedural word in a small project and I will use the game I am currently
developing with my company Mac n Cheese Games as an example on how to achieve this. Quick
introduction about myself. I have been working with video games for the last 20 years on every
possible console, mobile, VR, PC, next gen, you name it. I covered most of the positions
that exist in the realm of creating graphics for games. Most notable project was cyberpunk 2027
which I was a lead environmental artist. I learned a lot of things in that project and a lot of them
I pulled into this game we are developing. Today I am going to try to share the tricks I used to
create a procedure world that looks good. We know the problem with procedural when it comes to the
environment it often looks like it is a completely random. And it doesn't often look good. It is very
hard to place logic in the way procedural creates environment. I try to address these probs within
a reasonable budget with the tools we had. The game was developed and this is the trail for it.
It is not -- shameless promotion. Just trying to keep context. It is a meta roguelike game
in which you evolve into 30 different monsters, destroy a bunch of stuff, eat a bunch of humans,
and it is very action oriented. We are nearly ready to publish. It was developed I think around
two years and we are getting ready to probably be out, you know, in November. As I said,
it is a heavy metal roguelike. It is very art heavy. And Mac n Cheese Games games
which I am the founder of. We only have one 3D artist and that's me. I tried my best to
not go crazy while creating something that is worth looking at within the constraints of the
game design and the platform we were using. The main constraints are the fact this game features
five different biomes. And it is procedurally generated by procedurally arranging a library of
effects that are pre-addressed. We basically have a library of ties we address by hand.
I am going to show it to you in the next slide. Each of them is covered by a turn
of the destructive props. We had short time to deliver all of this. These tricks
we use it with were mostly directed at being fast and effective. As I mentioned before,
these are the 100 plus tiles we are using in the game. They are addressed by hand meaning we have
short time to take care of each one of them. At the same time, we wanted to deliver a game that
looked good. Our goal was mostly to have a dense single looking environment that would have been
a pleasure to destroy and at the same time we wanted to have it like super quick because we
just are such a team with a small timeframe so it had to be done quick. The main solution to this
was to use a good old technique kit bashing which is a technique that has been used since the time
of crafting things at home to make awesome mostly science fiction or historical miniatures and it
has been after using in the realm of computer graphics and video games. Basically describes
the act of taking a bunch of things that don't belong to each other and smash them together to
create something that is very complex. We did the same with our game. Instead of having a limited
library of like really unique good looking props that we would create as one piece, we decided to
create sets for each biome we have a set of 3-4 small sets. We combine them to create all the
props that are in that biome. Sometimes we take pieces from one set and use it in a different
biome but most of the time we are trying to keep them isolated and main thin the identity of each
biome. It is a process that starts slowly out of this reason you need to create the library but
speeds up exponentially your working time. We have a library for what is called the good swamp and on
the right is a sample of all the crops we created with those elements. Another problem was that we
had to set dress quickly the axis. We have 140 and needed to throw props at the X and then make sure
that they were looking good. You see there are two approaches. The one on top taking for the world of
war gain and models. And the second one where the props are basically already integrated with the
ground. So they kind of like blend in because in the proper it is contained a piece of the ground
and attention to the details of where the props get into tact with the surface that will host
it. We call it the props on their own feet. This is example from the game. The second one is the
same tree with a bunch of things, small pebbles, grass, smaller rock, and some moss that blends
it basically with the surface, the ground, and just like a flat plain. How do we do that? Like
we use basically three blending elements. One is the core of the object. The assets that compose
the prop. The second one is a base we created one for each environment. And at each prop lies
on that base and the other one is the bunch of simple props that are usually pebbles, grass,
and small bushes that surround the element so they basically create the gradient from the center
outside of the small clusters of object that tend to diminish in size and number. It is very
important to use class because it is something in nature. You don't distribute uniformly but bunch
them with the idea there are many small objects and chunks. The other principle we use is that we
had to keep the uniform variation and what does that mean? When you create a library of props
you cannot have all of them absolutely unique and to catch. Like they don't want them to distract
the player too much. You have to maintain them like uniform in the sense they don't scream for
attention too much. We create a set of small and medium generic props and then 3-4 hero pieces that
are basically props that really do want attention and are kind of unique and nicely decayed. What we
do is that we take each tile and try to place one or two hero props and surround them with
genetic props of the same volume. This is one of the typical tiles. You can see two error pieces
here. Then 2-3 medium props and then surrounded by small grass or bushes to blend them in. One
exception to these is the walls. You can see them on the top and bottom of this hex tiles as well.
And the walls were basically like blocks like single matches that contain everything that can
blend within the grounds. So like small pebbles or bones in the case of the triangle meshes.
And the logic is we just slam on the tile and they work out of the box. We don't have to adjust
because we need to place a lot of them and they have to be like considerably small low points.
This is what I use as, let's say, way of making sure the biomes, colors, gradients are compatible
as possible so a different area wouldn't feel out of a different game. I took a single camera and
used it to collect other five cameras that were proportionate to slices and each was looking at
the different biome and I would look through the camera while moving the objects around and
tweaking the materials so I would make sure that the whole look would be as, let's say, aligned as
possible between all the biomes. This is it. I hope that I was able to make possibly your
life easier in your project with these tweaks. Feel free to go on my website. Maxbottega.com
